# Cranial nerve palsies

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Peripheral nerve disorders > Cranial nerve palsies*

[Original Article Link](/library/tR0XKf)

---

## Summary

<u>Cranial nerve</u> palsy is characterized by a decreased or complete loss of function of one or more <u>cranial nerves</u>. <u>Cranial nerve</u> palsies can be congenital or acquired. Multiple <u>cranial</u> neuropathies are commonly caused by tumors, trauma, <u>ischemia</u>, or infections. While diagnosis can usually be made based on clinical features, further investigation is often warranted to determine the specific cause. Contrast-enhanced <u>MRI</u> is usually the preferred imaging modality to evaluate the affected nerve and any <u>soft tissue</u> abnormalities. A <u>CT scan</u> may be indicated to evaluate for bony lesions and <u>fractures</u> that may be compressing the nerve. Management is mainly aimed at treating the underlying cause. <u>Surgery</u> may be indicated for individuals with severe disability (e.g., acute traumatic <u>cranial nerve</u> palsies, persistent symptoms despite <u>conservative measures</u>). Spontaneous resolution over months may occur, especially in <u>cranial nerve</u> palsies secondary to microangiopathy.




<u>Facial nerve palsy</u> is covered in detail separately.

## Cranial nerve types and functions

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| II | Optic nerve | <br>* Sensory<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vision</u><br><br>* Afferent limb of the <u>pupillary light reflex</u><br><br><br> |
| III | Oculomotor nerve | <br>* Motor (somatic)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Eyelid</u> opening (indirect): <u>levator palpebrae superioris muscle</u><br><br>* <u>Eye</u> movement <br><br>* <u>Superior rectus muscle</u>: elevation, <u>intorsion</u>, and <u>adduction</u><br><br>* <u>Inferior rectus muscle</u>: <u>depression</u> and <u>extorsion</u><br><br>* <u>Medial rectus muscle</u>: <u>adduction</u><br><br>* <u>Inferior oblique muscle</u>: <u>extorsion</u>, elevation, and <u>abduction</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>* Motor (<u>parasympathetic</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pupillary</u> constriction<br><br>* <u>Pupillary sphincter</u> (Edinger-Westphal <u>nucleus</u> and <u>muscarinic receptors</u>)<br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>pupillary light reflex</u><br><br>* <u>Accommodation</u>: <u>ciliary muscle</u><br><br><br> |  |  |
| IV | Trochlear nerve | <br>* Motor<br><br> | <br>* <u>Eye</u> movement: <u>superior oblique muscle</u> (<u>intorsion</u>, <u>depression</u>, and <u>abduction</u>)   [[2]](/library/r_Xfp00)<br><br> |
| V | Trigeminal nerve | <br>* Sensory<br><br> | <br><br>* Facial sensation: ophthalmic (<u>CN V1</u>), maxillary (<u>CN V2</u>), <u>mandibular nerve</u> (<u>CN V3</u>)<br><br>* Innervation of:<br><br>* <u>Mucous membranes</u> of the oral and nasal cavity and the soft and <u>hard palate</u><br><br>* <u>Teeth</u><br><br>* <u>Temporomandibular joint</u><br><br>* <u>Meninges</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> wall of the <u>external auditory canal</u><br><br>* <u>Somatosensation</u> of <u>anterior</u> ⅔ of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Afferent limb of the corneal and <u>lacrimation reflexes</u> (nasociliary branch)<br><br>* Afferent limb of the <u>jaw jerk reflex</u> (<u>muscle spindle</u> from <u>masseter</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* Motor (only <u>mandibular nerve</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Muscles of mastication</u><br><br>* <u>Masseter</u>, <u>temporalis</u>, <u>medial pterygoid muscles</u> close the <u>jaw</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral pterygoid muscles</u> open the <u>jaw</u><br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>jaw jerk reflex</u> (<u>masseter</u>)<br><br>* Innervation of:<br><br>* <u>Tensor tympani muscle</u> (contraction dampens loud sounds)<br><br>* <u>Tensor veli palatini muscle</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> belly of the <u>digastric muscle</u><br><br>* Mylohyoid muscle<br><br><br> |  |  |
| VI | Abducens nerve | <br>* Motor<br><br> | <br>* <u>Eye</u> movement: <u>lateral rectus muscle</u>: <u>abduction</u><br><br> |
| VII | Facial nerve | <br>* Sensory<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Taste</u>: <u>anterior</u> ⅔ of the <u>tongue</u> (<u>chorda tympani</u>)<br><br>* Innervation of:<br><br>* <u>Tympanic membrane</u> (<u>chorda tympani</u>)<br><br>* <u>Skin</u> behind <u>the ear</u> (<u>posterior</u> auricular branch)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* Motor (somatic)<br><br> | <br><br>* Facial expression<br><br>* <u>Eyelid</u> closing: <u>orbicularis oculi muscle</u><br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>corneal reflex</u> (temporal branch, bilaterally)<br><br>* <u>Jaw</u> opening: <u>posterior</u> belly of the <u>digastric muscle</u><br><br>* Hyoid elevation: <u>stylohyoid muscle</u><br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>acoustic reflex</u> (<u>stapedius muscle</u>) → auditory volume modulation<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Motor (<u>parasympathetic</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Salivation: submandibular and <u>sublingual glands</u><br><br>* <u>Lacrimation</u>: <u>lacrimal gland</u><br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>lacrimation reflex</u><br><br><br> |  |  |
| VIII | Vestibulocochlear nerve | <br>* Sensory<br><br> | <br><br>* Balance and equilibrium: vestibular nerve<br><br>* <u>Hearing</u>: cochlear nerve<br><br><br> |
| IX | Glossopharyngeal nerve | <br>* Sensory<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Taste</u> perception: <u>posterior</u> ⅓ of the <u>tongue</u> (lingual branch)<br><br>* <u>Somatosensation</u>: <u>posterior</u> ⅓  of the <u>tongue</u>, <u>middle ear</u>, and <u>Eustachian tube</u> (tympanic nerve)<br><br>* Afferent limb of the <u>gag reflex</u><br><br>* <u>Visceral</u> sensation: <u>carotid sinus</u> (<u>baroreceptors</u> for blood pressure)<br><br>* Chemoreception: carotid body (<u>chemoreceptors</u> for <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>, <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>, and <u>pH</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* Motor (somatic)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Swallowing</u>: <u>pharyngeal muscles</u> (<u>CN IX</u> and <u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* Innervation of <u>stylopharyngeus muscle</u> (elevation of <u>pharynx</u>/<u>larynx</u>)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Motor (<u>parasympathetic</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Salivation: <u>parotid gland</u><br><br> |  |  |
| X | Vagus nerve | <br>* Sensory (somatic)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> wall of the <u>external auditory canal</u><br><br>* <u>Supraglottic</u> region, <u>larynx</u>, <u>trachea</u> (<u>cough reflex</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* Sensory (<u>visceral</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Taste</u> perception: <u>supraglottic</u> region<br><br>* <u>Visceral</u> sensation: aortic body (<u>baroreceptors</u> for blood pressure), <u>lung</u>, <u>stomach</u>, <u>liver</u>, <u>kidneys</u>, intestines up to left <u>colonic</u> flexure<br><br>* Chemoreception: aortic body (<u>chemoreceptors</u> for <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> and <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Motor (somatic)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Swallowing</u>: <u>pharyngeal muscles</u> (glossopharyngeal and <u>vagus nerves</u>)<br><br>* Middle and <u>inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles</u>: passage of bolus<br><br>* Palatoglossus muscle: elevates <u>posterior</u> <u>tongue</u> upon <u>swallowing</u><br><br>* Efferent limb of the <u>gag reflex</u><br><br>* Speech: laryngeal muscles (recurrent laryngeal branch)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Motor (<u>parasympathetic</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* SA and <u>AV node</u>: ↓ <u>heart rate</u><br><br>* <u>Blood vessels</u>: <u>vasodilation</u><br><br>* <u>Visceral</u> function: promotes the motility of the <u>esophagus</u>, <u>stomach</u>, intestines (up to the <u>splenic flexure</u>)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| XI | Accessory spinal nerve | <br>* Motor<br><br> | <br><br>* Head turn: <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u><br><br>* Shoulder elevation: <u>trapezius muscle</u><br><br><br> |
| XII | Hypoglossal nerve | <br>* Motor<br><br> | <br>* <u>Tongue</u> protrusion: intrinsic and <u>extrinsic muscles of the tongue</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> “Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brain Matters More:” <u>CN I</u> is sensory, <u>CN II</u> is sensory, <u>CN III</u> is motor, <u>CN IV</u> is motor, <u>CN V</u> is both (mixed), <u>CN VI</u> is motor, <u>CN VII</u> is both (mixed), <u>CN VIII</u> is sensory, <u>CN IX</u> is both (mixed), <u>CN X</u> is both (mixed), <u>CN XI</u> is motor, and <u>CN XII</u> is motor.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>CN VII</u> (Seven) controls Salivation by innervating Submandibular and Sublingual glands.

## Origin and pathways of the cranial nerves

### Gross anatomy




| <u>Origin and pathways of the cranial nerves</u> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Cranial nerve</u> | Nerve origin | Foramina/Structures | Cranial nerve nuclei | Destination | Pathway |
| <u>CN I</u> | <br>* <u>Olfactory epithelium</u> of the nasal <u>mucosa</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cribriform</u> plate<br><br> | <br>* -<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> <u>stria</u> → <u>telencephalon</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u> <u>stria</u> → <u>amygdala</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Olfactory receptor cells</u> (first order <u>neurons</u>) → fila olfactoria → penetrate <u>cribriform</u> plate of the <u>ethmoid bone</u> → <u>olfactory bulb</u> → <u>olfactory tract</u> (second order <u>neurons</u>) → (split into two) <u>lateral</u> portion connects directly with <u>telencephalon</u> (prepyriform area), <u>medial</u> portion connects with <u>amygdala</u>  [[3]](/library/VMYGnp)<br><br>* Only <u>cranial nerve</u> with no thalamic relay to cortex<br><br><br> |
| <u>CN II</u> | <br>* <u>Retinal ganglion cells</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Optic canal</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral geniculate nucleus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Visual cortex</u> on the <u>occipital lobe</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ganglion</u> cells of the <u>retina</u> → <u>optic nerve</u> → <u>optic canal</u> (<u>sphenoid</u> bone) → <u>optic chiasm</u> (<u>middle cranial fossa</u>) <br><br>* Fibers from nasal <u>retina</u>: cross at the <u>optic chiasm</u><br><br>* Fibers from temporal <u>retina</u>: continue ipsilaterally at the <u>optic chiasm</u><br><br>* <u>Optic chiasm</u> → <u>optic tract</u> → projects to <u>pretectal area</u>, <u>superior colliculi</u> , <u>suprachiasmatic nuclei</u>, and <u>lateral geniculate nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral geniculate nucleus</u> → optic radiation<br><br>* Upper <u>optic radiation</u>: fibers from superior retinal quadrants → <u>parietal lobe</u> → <u>visual cortex</u><br><br>* Lower <u>optic radiation</u>: fibers from inferior retinal quadrants → <u>temporal lobe</u> (<u>Meyer loop</u>) → <u>visual cortex</u><br><br>* <u>Visual cortex</u> on the <u>occipital lobe</u>: comprises the <u>calcarine sulcus</u> between lingual and cuneus <u>gyrus</u>  [[4]](/library/eMYxnp)<br><br><br> |
| <u>CN III</u> | <br>* <u>Midbrain</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> <u>cavernous sinus</u><br><br>* <u>Superior orbital fissure</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Somatic: oculomotor <u>nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Visceral</u>: Edinger-Westphal nucleus<br><br><br> | <br>* Ocular and orbital muscles<br><br> | <br><br>* Somatic: efferent fibers from oculomotor <u>nucleus</u> → <u>red nuclei</u> → <u>medial</u> aspect of the <u>cerebral peduncle</u><br><br>* <u>Visceral</u>: <u>Edinger-Westphal nucleus</u> → <u>preganglionic</u> <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers join <u>CN III</u> in the basilar segment<br><br>* Interpeduncular fossa → between <u>posterior cerebral artery</u> and <u>superior cerebellar artery</u> → <u>dura mater</u> → <u>lateral</u> wall of <u>cavernous sinus</u> → (together with <u>sympathetic</u> fibers from <u>internal carotid</u> plexus) <u>superior orbital fissure</u> → division into superior and inferior branch [[5]](/library/UMYbLp)<br><br>* Superior branch<br><br>* <u>Superior rectus</u> and <u>levator palpebrae superioris</u><br><br>* <u>Sympathetic</u> fibers → <u>superior tarsal muscle</u><br><br>* Inferior branch<br><br>* <u>Inferior rectus</u>, <u>medial rectus</u>, and <u>inferior oblique muscle</u><br><br>* <u>Preganglionic</u> <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers → <u>ciliary ganglion</u> → <u>sphincter pupillae</u> and <u>ciliary muscles</u><br><br><br> |

| <u>CN VIII</u> | <br>* <u>Internal auditory meatus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vestibular nuclei</u> complex<br><br>* <u>Ventral</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>cochlear nuclei</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cochlear pathway</u>: auditory cortex<br><br>* <u>Vestibular pathway</u>: vestibular cortex<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vestibular nuclei</u> complex and <u>ventral</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>cochlear nuclei</u> form the <u>vestibulocochlear nerve</u> → <u>internal auditory meatus</u> at the <u>cerebellopontine angle</u> → splits in vestibular nerve and the cochlear nerve  [[12]](/library/LMYw6p)<br><br>* Cochlear pathway: outer and inner <u>hair</u> cells (from the <u>organ of Corti</u>) → bipolar <u>neurons</u> of the spiral (cochlear) <u>ganglion</u> → cochlear nerve → <u>ventral</u> and <u>dorsal</u> <u>nuclei</u> → <u>superior olivary nucleus</u>  → <u>lateral lemniscus</u> → inferior colliculus → <u>medial geniculate body</u> → auditory radiations → <u>primary auditory cortex</u> (transverse temporal <u>gyri</u> of Heschl) and <u>amygdala</u> → auditory association cortex<br><br>* Vestibular pathway: <u>hair</u> cells of the <u>otolith organs</u>   and the three <u>semicircular canals</u>  → bipolar <u>neurons</u> of the <u>vestibular ganglion</u> → vestibular nerve → <u>vestibular nuclei</u> complex → <u>cerebellum</u> (<u>flocculonodular lobe</u>), <u>nuclei</u> of <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, and <u>CN VI</u> , <u>reticular formation</u> , spinal cord, and <u>thalamus</u> → vestibular cortex<br><br> |  |
| <u>CN IX</u> | <br>* Medulla<br><br> | <br>* <u>Jugular foramen</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inferior salivatory <u>nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Solitary nucleus</u><br><br>* Spinal <u>nucleus</u> of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Nucleus ambiguus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Pharyngeal <u>mucosa</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Postolivary sulcus</u> → <u>jugular foramen</u> (along with <u>CN X</u> and <u>CN XI</u>) → superior and inferior (petrous) <u>ganglia</u><br>* Tympanic nerve: sensory and <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers<br><br>* Sensory fibers to <u>middle ear</u>, internal surface of the <u>tympanic membrane</u>, and <u>Eustachian tube</u><br><br>* <u>Parasympathetic</u> fibers to <u>parotid gland</u><br><br>* Descends anterolateral to the <u>internal carotid artery</u><br><br>* Motor innervation of <u>stylopharyngeus muscle</u><br><br>* <u>Carotid sinus</u> nerve: sensory fibers to <u>carotid sinus</u> and body<br><br>* Enters <u>pharynx</u> between superior and <u>middle pharyngeal constrictors</u> [[13]](/library/KMYUpp)<br>* Divides into several sensory branches<br><br>* Unites with vagus fibers → pharyngeal plexus: sensory innervation of oropharyngeal <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* <u>Taste</u> and sensation to <u>posterior</u> ⅓ of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Tonsillar plexus: sensory innervation of <u>palatine tonsils</u><br><br><br> |

> [!NOTE]
> CN I–IV are located in the <u>midbrain</u>, V–VIII in the <u>pons</u>,and IX–XII in the medulla.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>nuclei</u> located in the <u>medial</u> <u>brainstem</u> are factors of 12, except 1 and 2 (i.e., <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, <u>CN VI</u>, and <u>CN XII</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> “Standing Room Only”: <u>CN V1</u> exits through Superior orbital <u>fissure</u>, <u>CN V2</u> exits through foramen Rotundum, and <u>CN V3</u> exits through foramen Ovale.




> [!NOTE]
> The sulcus limitans in the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> separates the CN Motor <u>nuclei</u> in the Medial part of the <u>brain stem</u> (<u>basal plate</u>) from the sensory <u>nuclei</u> in the Lateral part (aLar plate).

## Olfactory nerve palsy (I)

### Etiology




* Acquired

* Most commonly due to trauma to the <u>lateral</u> and occipital regions (e.g., <u>ethmoid bone</u> <u>fracture</u>)

* Intracranial space-occupying lesion (e.g., <u>meningioma</u>)

* Infection (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>)

* Congenital

* Primary: congenital <u>anosmia</u>

* Secondary in diseases such as <u>Kallmann syndrome</u> and <u>primary ciliary dyskinesia</u>





### Clinical features [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[19]](/library/5HXiIz)




* <u>Anosmia</u> (<u>hyposmia</u> or <u>dysosmia</u> may be present instead)

* Sudden <u>anosmia</u> typically occurs secondary to trauma.

* Progressively worsening <u>anosmia</u> is suggestive of an obstructive lesion or a <u>neurodegenerative disease</u>.

* Altered perception of <u>taste</u>





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[20]](/library/RLclx10)[[21]](/library/pCcLGe0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical and based on:




* Comprehensive history

* <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>: inability to identify certain smells (e.g., peppermint, coffee)  [[20]](/library/RLclx10)

* Assess for common differential diagnoses of olfactory dysfunction, such as sinonasal pathology. [[21]](/library/pCcLGe0)

* Perform a head and <u>neck exam</u>.

* Consult otolaryngology for <u>nasal endoscopy</u>.





#### Further evaluation [[20]](/library/RLclx10)




Evaluate for the underlying cause.




* Imaging [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[18]](/library/UXbbxH)

* CT maxillofacial region (with IV contrast): preferred for trauma or suspected sinonasal pathology not confirmed on <u>nasal endoscopy</u>

* <u>MRI</u> head (without and with IV contrast): preferred for a suspected primary neurological cause [[18]](/library/UXbbxH)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>eosinophil</u> count, <u>thyroid function tests</u>): to evaluate for other etiologies  as guided by clinical <u>probability</u>





### Treatment




* Consult <u>neurology</u>.

* Address any treatable causes identified.

* Consider a trial of olfactory training. [[20]](/library/RLclx10)[[22]](/library/Yd1nof0)[[23]](/library/Xd19of0)

* A self-administered therapy in which the patient exposes themselves to 4 different odors for ∼10 seconds twice daily for about 12–24 weeks.

* Associated with improved olfactory <u>sensitivity</u>, especially in olfactory dysfunction secondary to trauma and infections

* Spontaneous recovery (typically over months to years) can occur in up to half the patients with <u>anosmia</u>.  [[20]](/library/RLclx10)[[21]](/library/pCcLGe0)





> [!TIP]
> Counsel patients on <u>coping strategies</u> such as monitoring for signs of spoiled food and installing smoke and gas detectors. [[24]](/library/JKcshW0)




![Olfactory groove meningioma](media/xcdw5go3wihaxd7ywsi8ke1t.jpg)

## Optic nerve palsy (II)

### Etiology




* Acquired

* <u>Ischemic</u> optic neuropathy (i.e., caused by <u>microvascular</u> disease, <u>giant cell arteritis</u>)

* Inflammation (<u>optic neuritis</u>): <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, viral infections (e.g., <u>measles</u>, <u>mumps</u>)

* Trauma

* Tumors: e.g., <u>optic nerve</u> <u>glioma</u>, <u>pituitary adenoma</u>

* <u>Elevated intracranial pressure</u>: e.g., <u>hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Malnutrition</u>: <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>

* Drugs: <u>sildenafil</u>, <u>amiodarone</u>, <u>ethambutol</u>

* Toxins: e.g., ethyl <u>alcohol</u>, <u>mercury</u>, lead

* Congenital

* Primary: <u>optic nerve</u> <u>hypoplasia</u>

* Secondary: infantile <u>nystagmus</u>, sensory <u>strabismus</u>





### Clinical features [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)




* Impaired <u>vision</u>, including blindness (may start as <u>night blindness</u>), depending on the site of the lesion

* Features of the underlying disease, such as: [[25]](/library/Z6cZjW0)

* <u>Uhthoff phenomenon</u> in <u>multiple sclerosis</u>

* <u>Jaw claudication</u> and <u>headache</u> in <u>giant cell arteritis</u>





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[25]](/library/Z6cZjW0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical and based on a <u>comprehensive ocular examination</u> as part of the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>, which includes:




* Assessment of <u>pupillary</u> response, <u>visual field exam</u>, and <u>visual acuity</u> tests

* Complete transection: <u>ipsilateral</u> blindness and loss of direct and <u>indirect pupillary reflex</u>  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)

* <u>Pituitary adenoma</u> (compression to the <u>optic chiasm</u>): <u>bitemporal hemianopia</u>  [[4]](/library/eMYxnp)

* Unilateral <u>optic nerve</u> dysfunction: <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u> [[25]](/library/Z6cZjW0)[[26]](/library/F1bgis)

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>: findings depend on the underlying cause and include

* <u>Papillitis</u>

* <u>Papilledema</u> in <u>↑ ICP</u>

* <u>Optic atrophy</u> in compression (e.g., <u>tumor</u>)





#### Further evaluation[[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)




Consider further evaluation for underlying cause based on clinical findings.




* Imaging [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)

* CT head (without IV contrast): initial evaluation of trauma or orbital <u>complications of sinusitis</u>

* <u>MRI</u> head and <u>orbits</u> (with IV contrast): initial evaluation of suspected <u>tumor</u>, <u>optic neuritis</u>, or <u>neurodegenerative diseases</u>

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> to evaluate for the underlying cause (as guided by clinical <u>probability</u>); examples include: [[28]](/library/XNY9-6)[[29]](/library/a6cQjW0)

* <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* <u>ANA</u> and <u>antigen-specific ANAs</u>

* Toxic exposure tests

### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[25]](/library/Z6cZjW0)




* Address any underlying etiologies identified.

* Consult neurosurgery and/or ophthalmology.

* Traumatic <u>CN II</u> palsy: Options include <u>surgery</u>, high-dose <u>corticosteroids</u>, and observation.

## Oculomotor nerve palsy (III)

### Etiology




| Etiology of <u>CN III palsy</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Cause | Clinical features |
| Oculomotor <u>nuclei</u> | <br><br>* <u>Ischemic stroke</u> (<u>posterior cerebral artery</u>)<br><br>* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* The <u>corticospinal tract</u> is usually also affected, causing syndromes characterized by <u>ipsilateral</u> oculomotor palsy and <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemiparesis</u>:<br><br>* <u>Benedikt syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Weber syndrome</u><br><br>* Unilateral lesion of the oculomotor <u>nucleus</u> can cause bilateral <u>superior rectus muscle</u> palsy.  [[30]](/library/tMbXq8)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Basilar segment<br> | <br><br>* <u>Aneurysm</u> of the <u>posterior communicating artery</u><br><br>* <u>Skull base fracture</u><br><br>* Basal <u>meningitis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* <u>Paralytic squint</u><br><br>* <u>Pupillary</u> involvement: nonreactive, <u>dilated pupil</u> (<u>blown pupil</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Transtentorial herniation</u> (<u>uncal herniation</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Abducens nerve palsy</u><br><br>* <u>Features of elevated intracranial pressure</u> (e.g., <u>coma</u>, <u>blown pupil</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hutchinson pupil</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Intracavernous segment | <br><br>* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u><br><br>* <u>Tolosa-Hunt syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Internal carotid artery</u> <u>aneurysms</u><br><br>* Large parasellar tumors (e.g., <u>meningioma</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>CN IV</u>, <u>CN V</u> (<u>CN V1</u>, <u>CN V2</u>), and/or <u>CN VI palsy</u><br><br> |
| Intraorbital segment | <br><br>* Tumors within the orbital cavity<br><br>* Trauma<br><br>* <u>Orbital cellulitis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Loss of <u>vision</u><br><br>* <u>Pain</u><br><br>* <u>Proptosis</u><br><br>* Palsies associated with <u>CN IV</u> and/or <u>CN VI</u><br><br>* Nonreactive <u>pupil</u><br><br><br> |
| Isolated <u>oculomotor nerve palsy</u> | <br><br>* <u>Ischemic</u> microangiopathy (e.g., diabetic <u>cranial</u> mononeuropathy, <u>hypertension</u>)<br><br>* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u><br><br>* <u>Myasthenia gravis</u><br><br>* <u>Giant cell arteritis</u><br><br>* High-speed deceleration injuries [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Paralytic squint</u><br><br>* <u>Pupillary</u> involvement: typically sparing the <u>pupil</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Parasympathetic</u> fibers of <u>CN III</u> are located superficially and motor fibers are located centrally. <u>Parasympathetic</u> fibers are more susceptible to compressive lesions (e.g., <u>uncal herniation</u>, <u>aneurysm</u> of the <u>posterior communicating artery</u>). Motor fibers are more susceptible to <u>ischemia</u> (e.g., <u>vasculitis</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, <u>atherosclerosis</u>).




### Clinical features [[31]](/library/c6caPW0)




* Horizontal <u>diplopia</u> that worsens when the head is turned away from the side of the lesion

* <u>Ptosis</u>

* Light <u>sensitivity</u>

* Additional features may be present, depending on the cause and the level of the <u>oculomotor nerve lesion</u>.





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical and based on a <u>comprehensive ocular examination</u> as part of the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* <u>Assessment of extraocular muscle function</u>  : Lesions of the motor portion typically produce <u>paralytic squint</u>.  

* Down-and-out gaze: affected <u>eye</u> looks outwards (<u>exotropia</u>) and downwards (<u>hypotropia</u>)

* <u>Adduction</u> <u>weakness</u>

* Assessment of <u>pupillary</u> response (afferent: <u>CN II</u>; efferent: <u>CN III</u>)  

* Lesions of the autonomic (<u>parasympathetic</u>) portion result in loss of the <u>pupillary reflex</u>.

* See also “<u>Physiology and abnormalities of the pupil</u>” for details on <u>oculomotor nerve lesions</u> and drugs that affect <u>pupillary</u> size.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Oculomotor nerve palsy</u> leaves you down and out.




> [!TIP]
> Impaired <u>pupillary reaction</u> with relative sparing of <u>motor function</u> is typically seen in compressive lesions. Prominent motor dysfunction with sparing of the <u>pupil</u> is typically seen in <u>ischemic</u> lesions. However, <u>pupillary</u> findings cannot reliably distinguish between the etiologies of oculomotor palsy. [[28]](/library/XNY9-6)[[32]](/library/RoclbW0)[[33]](/library/I7cYMd0)




![Clinical testing of the extraocular muscles](media/vye8c2e6m8qxo35s0aw48t45.jpg)

Clinical testing of the extraocular muscles

![Pupillary light reflex](media/bw2progeabym6wu4uerual5p.jpg)

Pupillary light reflex

![Right-sided Oculomotor Nerve Palsy](media/small_609bc25677da7.jpg)

Right-sided Oculomotor Nerve Palsy

![Oculomotor nerve palsy](media/wy1mk5y780565we9gych0prx.jpg)

Oculomotor nerve palsy

![Bilateral complete oculomotor palsy](media/z944w71kkbfkb2dlw8c0uxi9.jpg)

Bilateral complete oculomotor palsy




#### Further evaluation




Evaluate for underlying cause based on clinical findings.




| <br>Workup for suspected <u>CN III palsy</u> [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clinical findings | Likely underlying cause | Further evaluation |
| Complete palsy with <u>dilated pupil</u><br>OR<br>Incomplete palsy regardless of <u>pupillary</u> findings | <br>* Suggestive of a compressive lesion (e.g., <u>posterior communicating artery</u> <u>aneurysm</u>) [[31]](/library/c6caPW0)<br><br> | <br><br>* Obtain urgent <u>MRI</u> head (without and with IV contrast) with <u>MR angiography</u>  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)[[32]](/library/RoclbW0)[[34]](/library/td1X7f0)<br><br>* Consult neurosurgery depending on findings.<br><br>* If <u>MRI</u> is normal, consult <u>neurology</u> and/or ophthalmology and consider a <u>lumbar puncture</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Complete palsy with a normal <u>pupillary reflex</u> (<u>pupillary</u> sparing) | <br>* Suggestive of <u>ischemic</u> microangiopathy, especially in patients > 50 years of age with <u>atherosclerotic risk factors</u> [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)[[35]](/library/U9cb5e0)<br><br> | <br><br>* Initial <u>neuroimaging</u> may not be routinely required.  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)[[32]](/library/RoclbW0)[[33]](/library/I7cYMd0)<br><br>* Consult <u>neurology</u> and/or ophthalmology.<br><br>* Assess <u>risk factors for atherosclerosis</u> or arteritis; e.g., [[31]](/library/c6caPW0)<br><br>* Check blood pressure and blood <u>glucose</u>.<br><br>* Consider additional <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>ESR</u>, <u>lipid profile</u>, <u>ANA</u>, <u>syphilis diagnostics</u>) as needed.<br><br>* Consider <u>MRI</u> head (without and with IV contrast) if signs of <u>pupillary</u> involvement develop, or if there is no recovery after 6–8 weeks.  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>MRI</u> <u>orbits</u> (without and with IV contrast) should be obtained in patients with <u>ophthalmoplegia</u> and a history of trauma, or those with evidence of orbital injury or inflammation (i.e., enopthalmos, <u>proptosis</u>, <u>chemosis</u>). [[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>MRI</u> head should also be obtained in patients ≤ 50 years old with a history of cancer and additional neurologic findings, including nonisolated <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy. [[34]](/library/td1X7f0)




### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)




* Compressive lesions

* Immediate neurosurgery referral for management

* <u>Posterior communicating artery</u> <u>aneurysm</u> requires urgent neurosurgical <u>clipping</u> or <u>endovascular coiling</u>  [[36]](/library/QEcuvV0)[[37]](/library/e9cxme0)

* Consider <u>strabismus surgery</u> if symptoms do not improve after treatment of the underlying cause.

* <u>Ischemic</u> microangiopathy or <u>demyelinating</u> lesions

* Medical management with control of the underlying disease

* <u>Ischemic</u> <u>CN III palsy</u> typically resolves spontaneously within 6–8 weeks. [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[31]](/library/c6caPW0)

* <u>Prism glasses</u> or an <u>eye</u> patch can be used to improve <u>diplopia</u> while awaiting resolution.





> [!NOTE]
> Motor fibers are in the Middle of <u>CN III</u>, while Parasympathetic fibers are on the Periphery of the nerve.

---

## Trochlear nerve palsy (IV)

### Etiology




* Acquired

* <u>Microvascular</u> damage (<u>diabetes</u>, <u>hypertension</u>, <u>arteriosclerosis</u>)

* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u>

* Trauma

* Congenital: fourth nerve palsy





### Clinical features




* Vertical or oblique <u>diplopia</u>

* Exacerbated on downgaze (e.g., reading, walking downstairs) away from side of affected muscle [[38]](/library/1d12Kf0)

* Worsens when patient turns the head towards the paralyzed muscle → compensatory head tilt to the opposite side of the lesion





> [!NOTE]
> With damage to the <u>CN IV</u>, you cannot look at the floor.




![Hypertropia](media/ibbukw1wggghhtxkzfblajo2.jpg)

Hypertropia




### Diagnostics




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on <u>cranial nerve examination</u>, which includes: [[38]](/library/1d12Kf0)[[39]](/library/G7cBMd0)




* <u>Assessment of extraocular muscle function</u> 

* <u>Extorsion</u> of the <u>eye</u>

* Inability to depress and <u>adduct</u> the eyeball simultaneously

* <u>Park-Bielchowsky test</u>: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>hypertropia</u> that worsens on <u>contralateral</u> gaze and <u>ipsilateral</u> head tilt





![Clinical testing of the extraocular muscles](media/vye8c2e6m8qxo35s0aw48t45.jpg)

Clinical testing of the extraocular muscles

![Right-sided trochlear nerve palsy](media/small_609bc34a0ed1d.jpg)

Right-sided trochlear nerve palsy

![Trochlear nerve palsy](media/pnjckthe0s7ohtyjz4r96i74.jpg)

Trochlear nerve palsy

![Trochlear nerve palsy](media/y8jkgfb6xjrtc7tw4svmyfvx.jpg)

Trochlear nerve palsy




#### Imaging [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[27]](/library/RU1l1T0)[[34]](/library/td1X7f0)




* Not routinely required

* Consider <u>MRI</u> head and <u>orbits</u> (without and with IV contrast) in consultation with a <u>neurologist</u> in the following situations

* History of trauma

* Patients ≤ 50 years old with a history of cancer and additional neurologic findings, including nonisolated <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy

* Persistent palsy after 3 months (in all age groups)

* Progression of symptoms





### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[40]](/library/Wd1PKf0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and ophthalmology.

* Symptoms often resolve spontaneously within six months of onset.

* <u>Prism glasses</u> or an <u>eye</u> patch can be used to improve <u>diplopia</u> while awaiting resolution.

* Surgical realignment may be needed for persistent <u>CN IV palsy</u>.

---

## Trigeminal nerve palsy (V)

### Etiology




* <u>Tumor</u>

* Vascular compression

* Trauma, including maxillofacial or oral <u>surgery</u>, and mandibular molar extractions

* Inflammation of the nerve

* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u>





### Clinical features




Clinical features depend on the site of the lesion and can include (see “<u>Localizing features of CN V palsy</u>” for details):




* Altered sensation over the face and <u>tongue</u>

* <u>Weakness</u> in <u>muscles of mastication</u>

* <u>Hearing</u> impairment





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[41]](/library/C6cqMW0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on <u>ear examination</u>, <u>nose and throat examination</u>, and <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* Assess for decreased facial sensation to <u>light touch</u>, <u>pain</u> (can also be increased), and/or temperature (<u>CN V1</u>, V2).

* Assess for diminished/absent <u>corneal reflex</u> or <u>lacrimation reflex</u> (<u>CN V1</u>).

* Assess <u>muscles of mastication</u> (<u>CN V3</u>) for:

* Signs of <u>atrophy</u>

* Decreased strength (e.g., open mouth against resistance)

* <u>Jaw jerk reflex</u>





| Localizing features of CN V palsy |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peripheral <u>trigeminal nerve</u> lesions | <u>Ophthalmic nerve</u> (<u>CN V1</u>) | <br><br>* Absent <u>corneal reflex</u> (afferent limb)<br><br>* Loss of sensation in the <u>ipsilateral</u> forehead<br><br><br> |
| <u>Maxillary nerve</u> (<u>CN V2</u>) | <br>* Loss of sensation in the <u>ipsilateral</u> midface<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Mandibular nerve</u> (<u>CN V3</u>)<br> | <br><br>* Anesthesia of the <u>ipsilateral</u> lower ⅓ of the face and <u>anterior</u> ⅔ of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* <u>Paresis</u> of <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>muscles of mastication</u> <br><br>* Deviation of <u>jaw</u> towards the side of the lesion due to unopposed action from the opposite pterygoid muscle<br><br>* Diminished/absent <u>jaw jerk reflex</u> (<u>CN V3</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| Lesion of the <u>tensor tympani</u> branch |  | <br>* <u>Hearing</u> impairment (particularly affecting low-pitched sounds)<br><br> |
| <br>Lesions of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u> <u>nuclei</u> (depending on the <u>nuclei</u> affected) <br> |  | <br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> <u>weakness</u> of <u>muscles of mastication</u> and/or <u>ipsilateral</u> loss of sensation<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The primary features of <u>trigeminal</u> neuropathy are numbness and/or <u>weakness</u> in the areas of <u>trigeminal nerve</u> innervation, whereas the primary feature of <u>trigeminal neuralgia</u> is intermittent sharp <u>pain</u> in the same area without sensory or motor deficits. [[41]](/library/C6cqMW0)




![Cutaneous innervation of the trigeminal nerve](media/rozks5tfco2u6ingifc8dspz.jpg)

Cutaneous innervation of the trigeminal nerve

![Innervation of the tongue](media/gcibn7youzj7ul56wsmy1yi1.jpg)

Innervation of the tongue




#### Further evaluation




Consider further evaluation for underlying cause based on clinical findings.




* Imaging [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[41]](/library/C6cqMW0)

* Not routinely required if the underlying cause is clear (e.g., peripheral <u>paresthesia</u> following mandibular molar extraction)

* History of <u>head trauma</u>: Consider CT head and <u>skull base</u>.

* Suspected <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>, <u>tumor</u>, <u>cavernous sinus thrombosis</u> : <u>MRI</u> head (without and with IV contrast)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> (as needed): e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>ESR</u>, <u>RPR</u>, <u>ANA</u> and <u>antigen-specific ANAs</u>





### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[41]](/library/C6cqMW0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and maxillofacial <u>surgery</u>.

* Traumatic <u>CN V palsy</u> (e.g., following dental <u>surgery</u>) often resolves spontaneously within six months of symptom onset.

* Consider <u>adjuvant analgesics</u> as needed for <u>pain</u>.

* Treat the underlying cause (e.g., see “<u>Treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis</u>”).

* Screen for and treat complications.

* Monitor for <u>tongue</u> and mouth injuries due to decreased sensation.

* Screen for inadequate nutrition due to weak <u>mastication</u>.

* Consider <u>biofeedback training</u> for <u>chronic pain</u> and <u>weakness</u>.

* Screen for corneal <u>edema</u> due to absent <u>corneal reflex</u>; consider protective contact lenses.

* Screen for <u>symptoms of depression</u>.

---

## Abducens nerve palsy (VI)

### Etiology [[10]](/library/TMY6Lp)[[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)




* Acquired

* Trauma (e.g., at the <u>superior orbital fissure</u>)

* <u>Pseudotumor cerebri</u>

* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u>

* Space-occupying lesion causing downward pressure (e.g., <u>tumor</u>)

* <u>Diabetic neuropathy</u>

* <u>Giant cell arteritis</u> (<u>GCA</u>)

* Congenital: Duane syndrome (a rare type of <u>strabismus</u> characterized by an impaired <u>abduction</u> and <u>ptosis</u> on <u>adduction</u>) [[43]](/library/wOahuk)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Abducens nerve palsy</u> is the most common ocular <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy.




### Clinical features




* Horizontal <u>diplopia</u> that worsens when looking at distant objects

* Inability to look laterally in the affected <u>eye</u>

* Features of the underlying cause





### Diagnostics [[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)[[44]](/library/ZHcZKd0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on the <u>examination of the extraocular muscles</u> as part of the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* <u>Esotropia</u>: <u>medial</u> deviation of the affected <u>eye</u> at <u>primary gaze</u>

* Inability to <u>abduct</u> the affected <u>eye</u>





![Right-sided Abducens Nerve Palsy](media/small_609bbeaf1545c.jpg)

Right-sided Abducens Nerve Palsy

![Abducens nerve palsy](media/ababagj3ectz05m7myrgea7a.jpg)

Abducens nerve palsy

![Abducens nerve palsy](media/iqd9glyllyq0l0iuj9ordxfb.jpg)

Abducens nerve palsy




#### Further evaluation [[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)




Evaluate for underlying cause based on clinical findings.




* <u>MRI</u> head and <u>orbits</u> (with IV contrast) if any of the following are present:  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[34]](/library/td1X7f0)[[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)[[44]](/library/ZHcZKd0)

* Patients < 50 years of age

* History of cancer

* No <u>ischemic</u> <u>risk factors</u>

* Additional neurologic findings, including nonisolated <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy

* No evidence of resolution after 3 months

* Evaluation of all other patients (or patients with normal <u>neuroimaging</u>): [[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)[[44]](/library/ZHcZKd0)

* Consult <u>neurology</u> and/or ophthalmology.

* Assess for <u>ischemic</u> <u>risk factors</u> : e.g., Check blood pressure, blood <u>glucose</u>, <u>lipid profile</u>, <u>ESR</u>.

* Assess for underlying infection, autoimmune etiologies, or mimics (e.g., <u>thyroid</u> <u>eye</u> disease, <u>myasthenia gravis</u>) as needed.

* <u>CBC</u>, <u>ANA</u>

* <u>Syphilis diagnostics</u>,

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>, <u>AChR antibody</u> levels

* Consider <u>lumbar puncture</u>.





### Treatment




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and ophthalmology.

* Treat the underlying cause.

* Complete resolution of isolated <u>CN VI palsy</u> is seen in 75–88% of patients within 6 months of symptom onset. [[42]](/library/x6cEMW0)

* <u>Prism glasses</u> or <u>eye</u> patching may be considered to manage disabling <u>diplopia</u>.

* Consider <u>strabismus surgery</u> for chronic <u>CN VI palsy</u>.[[45]](/library/6ocj1W0)

---

## Facial nerve palsy (VII)

* See “<u>Facial nerve palsy</u>.”

---

## Vestibulocochlear nerve palsy (VIII)

### Etiology




* <u>Bacterial meningitis</u> (most common <u>cranial nerve</u> palsy)

* <u>Lyme disease</u>

* <u>Tumor</u> (e.g., <u>acoustic neuroma</u>, <u>neurofibromatosis type 2</u>)

* Trauma: <u>basilar skull fracture</u> (damage to the <u>CN VIII</u> within the <u>internal acoustic meatus</u> → symptoms of vestibular and cochlear nerve damage)





### Clinical features




* <u>Hearing loss</u>

* <u>Vertigo</u>

* <u>Motion sickness</u> [[46]](/library/COaquk)

* <u>Tinnitus</u>





### Diagnostics [[47]](/library/y6cdnW0)[[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on a comprehensive <u>examination of the ears</u>, <u>hearing</u>, and <u>vestibular system</u>, as part of the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* Evaluation of cochlear nerve function (<u>Rinne test</u>, <u>Weber test</u>, <u>audiometry</u>) : <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>

* Evaluation of vestibular nerve function (<u>HINTS exam</u>, <u>vestibular function tests</u>): features of <u>peripheral vertigo</u> (see “<u>Peripheral vs. central vertigo</u>”)

* Abnormal <u>head impulse test</u>

* <u>Horizontal nystagmus</u>; gaze fixation suppresses <u>nystagmus</u>

* <u>Skew deviation</u> is absent





> [!TIP]
> If a tuning fork is unavailable, a <u>hum test</u> may be used as an alternative to the <u>Weber test</u> [[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)




> [!TIP]
> In patients with sudden <u>hearing loss</u>, <u>audiometry</u> should be performed within 14 days from the onset of symptoms. [[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)




#### Further evaluation




Consider further evaluation for underlying cause based on clinical findings.




* <u>Laboratory studies</u> as needed: e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>ANA</u>, or testing for <u>Lyme disease</u>, <u>syphilis</u>, <u>TB</u>, or <u>HIV</u>

* Imaging: <u>MRI</u> head and <u>brainstem</u> with IV contrast (to assess for, e.g., <u>vestibular schwannoma</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, <u>TIA</u>)  [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)





### Treatment [[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and/or otolaryngology.

* Treatment is aimed at resolving underlying causes (e.g., surgical excision and/or radiation for a <u>tumor</u>).

* Consider <u>expectant management</u> with scheduled repeat <u>audiometry</u> to assess for spontaneous recovery.

* For severe <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>, consider initial treatment with <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE within two weeks of symptom onset. [[48]](/library/YHcnKd0)

---

## Glossopharyngeal nerve palsy (IX)

### Etiology




* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Compression (e.g., <u>aneurysm</u>, <u>tumor</u>, <u>retropharyngeal abscess</u>)

* Trauma (<u>skull base fractures</u>)





### Clinical features




Isolated <u>CN IX</u> palsy is rare and may be asymptomatic due to shared sensory and motor <u>nuclei</u> with adjacent nerves. [[49]](/library/SKayfl)




* Throat and <u>ear</u> <u>pain</u> (glossopharyngeal <u>neuralgia</u>)

* Mild <u>dysphagia</u>

* Altered <u>taste</u> over the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the <u>tongue</u>

* Difficulty <u>swallowing</u>





> [!TIP]
> Lesions that affect the <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> typically also affect the <u>vagus nerve</u> because the two nerves exit the <u>jugular foramen</u> in close proximity. [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[49]](/library/SKayfl)




### Diagnostics [[49]](/library/SKayfl)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* <u>Ipsilateral</u> diminished or absent gag response (afferent limb).

* Loss of <u>taste</u> in the <u>posterior</u> third of the <u>tongue</u>.

* Sensory loss over the <u>soft palate</u>, upper <u>pharynx</u>, and <u>posterior</u> third of the <u>tongue</u> (including loss of <u>taste</u> sensation)





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>carotid sinus</u> <u>baroreceptors</u> are innervated by the <u>carotid sinus</u> nerve, a branch of the <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u>. Injury to the <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> may result in impairment of the <u>baroreceptor reflex</u>. [[50]](/library/HU1KeT0)




![Innervation of the tongue](media/gcibn7youzj7ul56wsmy1yi1.jpg)

Innervation of the tongue




#### Further evaluation



* Consider high-resolution <u>MRI</u> <u>orbit</u>, face, and neck, in conjunction with <u>MRI</u> head (without and with IV contrast) to assess for underlying cause. [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[18]](/library/UXbbxH)[[51]](/library/k9cmne0)




### Treatment




* Consults [[49]](/library/SKayfl)

* <u>Neurology</u> for all patients

* Otolaryngology for patients with laryngeal or pharyngeal symptoms (for <u>laryngoscopy</u>)

* <u>Speech therapy</u> as needed

* Address suspected underlying cause if identified.

* Consider <u>acute pain management</u> with <u>adjuvant analgesics</u> for glossopharyngeal <u>neuralgia</u>. [[51]](/library/k9cmne0)

---

## Vagus nerve palsy (X)

### Etiology




* Trauma (<u>skull base fractures</u>)

* <u>Diabetes</u>

* Inflammation

* <u>Aortic aneurysms</u>

* <u>Neurodegenerative conditions</u>

* Tumors

* <u>Surgery</u> (e.g, recurrent nerve injury during <u>thyroidectomy</u>)





![Thyroid gland and surrounding structures](media/vkwwlt3ct90xv3iwa62w4ioo.jpg)

Thyroid gland and surrounding structures




### Clinical features




* Nasal speech

* <u>Dysphagia</u>, <u>aspiration</u>

* Vocal cord paralysis, manifesting as:

* Dysphonia (<u>hoarseness</u>) in unilateral <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u> palsy

* Aphonia and <u>inspiratory stridor</u> in bilateral <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u> palsy

* Features of <u>gastroparesis</u>, e.g., <u>postprandial</u> <u>bloating</u>





> [!TIP]
> Unilateral <u>vocal cord paralysis</u> may be asymptomatic due to compensation from the <u>contralateral</u> <u>vocal cord</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Lesions that affect the <u>vagus nerve</u> typically also affect the <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> because the two nerves exit the <u>jugular foramen</u> in close proximity. [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[49]](/library/SKayfl)




### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[49]](/library/SKayfl)[[52]](/library/hHccJd0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




* Perform a focused <u>HEENT examination</u> and <u>cranial nerve examination</u>, assessing for:

* Diminished or absent <u>gag reflex</u> (efferent limb) and/or <u>cough reflex</u> (afferent limb; impulses travel via the <u>internal laryngeal nerve</u>)

* Uvular deviation: Articulating "ahh" will cause the uvula to deviate away from the affected side.

* <u>Flaccid paralysis</u> and <u>ipsilateral</u> lowering of <u>soft palate</u>

* Pharyngeal dysfunction: Ask the patient to swallow some water; choking or difficulty <u>swallowing</u> indicated dysfunction.

* <u>Tachycardia</u> (<u>resting heart rate</u> > 100 beats per minute)

* Observe the patient's breathing and voice, assessing for: [[52]](/library/hHccJd0)

* <u>Stridor</u>: May indicate bilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u>; perform immediate <u>airway management</u> and consult otolaryngology.

* <u>Dysphonia</u>: <u>Hoarseness</u> is suggestive of unilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u>; aphonia is suggestive of bilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u>.

* <u>Dysarthria</u>: <u>Dysphonia</u> with <u>dysarthria</u> and <u>dysphagia</u> may indicate neurological pathology (e.g., <u>amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>).

* Consult otolaryngology for evaluation of <u>larynx</u> and <u>pharynx</u>, including: [[49]](/library/SKayfl)[[52]](/library/hHccJd0)

* <u>Laryngoscopy</u> (direct and indirect): to identify <u>vocal cord palsy</u> (unilateral or bilateral)

* <u>Fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy</u>: to evaluate the <u>upper respiratory tract</u> for structural abnormalities or foreign bodies





> [!TIP]
> Isolated palsy of the <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>(s) indicates that the site of the lesion is most likely <u>distal</u> to the <u>hyoid bone</u>. More <u>proximal</u> lesions manifest with <u>dysphagia</u>, nasal speech, palatal <u>paralysis</u>, and uvular deviation. [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[49]](/library/SKayfl)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Dysphonia</u> in a patient with a neck mass, <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>stridor</u>, progressive neurological symptoms, history of tobacco use, or history of <u>surgery</u> on the head, neck, or chest requires urgent evaluation by an otolaryngology specialist to evaluate for a potentially serious underlying cause. [[52]](/library/hHccJd0)




![Vocal cord paralysis](media/hk648lbpzxytxzlffqgnx6xb.jpg)

Vocal cord paralysis




#### Further evaluation [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[18]](/library/UXbbxH)




Based on clinical and laryngoscopic findings, consult <u>neurology</u> and consider further evaluation, including:




* <u>MRI</u> head and <u>brainstem</u> (without and with IV contrast): to evaluate for <u>proximal</u> or intracranial etiologies, such as <u>stroke</u> or <u>neoplasms</u>

* CT neck and <u>proximal</u> chest (with IV contrast): to evaluate for <u>distal</u> causes, such as <u>thyroid</u>, neck mass, or <u>thoracic aortic aneurysm</u>





### Treatment [[49]](/library/SKayfl)[[52]](/library/hHccJd0)




Treatment varies depending on the cause and severity of symptoms; options include the following:




* <u>Expectant management</u>: Patients with <u>dysphonia</u> of unclear cause may be observed for up to 4 weeks if no indications for expedited <u>laryngoscopy</u> are present.

* Voice therapy: may be performed alone or in conjunction with <u>surgery</u>  [[53]](/library/Ce1qaT0)

* <u>Surgery</u> [[54]](/library/zd1rsf0)

* Unilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u>: interventions to reduce the <u>glottic</u> opening (e.g., injection laryngoplasty)  or thyroplasty

* Bilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u>: <u>tracheostomy</u> or interventions to enlarge the <u>glottic</u> opening (e.g., <u>lateral</u> fixation of the <u>vocal fold</u>, arytenoidectomy, and/or cordotomy)





> [!WARNING]
> Bilateral <u>vocal cord palsy</u> with <u>stridor</u> and <u>dyspnea</u> is a potentially <u>airway</u>-threatening condition. Consult otolaryngology urgently to <u>secure the airway</u> (e.g., via <u>tracheostomy</u>). [[54]](/library/zd1rsf0)

---

## Accessory nerve palsy (XI)

### Etiology




* <u>Iatrogenic</u>: most commonly from <u>surgery</u> of <u>lateral cervical region</u>; , especially <u>posterior</u> border of <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u> (e.g., resection of <u>posterior</u> cervical <u>lymph nodes</u>, radical <u>neck dissection</u>)

* Trauma (e.g., <u>sternoclavicular joint</u> <u>dislocation</u>, <u>acromioclavicular joint dislocation</u>)

* <u>Tumor</u>





### Clinical features [[55]](/library/LJcwuW0)




* Shoulder <u>pain</u> and heaviness

* Difficulty or inability to raise hand <u>overhead</u>

* Neckline asymmetry





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)[[17]](/library/29cT5e0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>.




* Inspect upper back, shoulder, and neck

* <u>Paresis</u>, <u>atrophy</u>, and/or asymmetry of the <u>trapezius muscle</u> 

* <u>Ipsilateral</u> shoulder drooping

* <u>Lateral</u> <u>winging of the scapula</u>

* <u>Paresis</u>, <u>atrophy</u>, and/or asymmetry of the <u>sternocleidomastoid</u>

* Assess the <u>trapezius muscle</u>.

* Ask the patient to shrug their shoulders.

* <u>CN XI</u> palsy results in <u>weakness</u> during elevation of the <u>ipsilateral</u> shoulder.

* Assess the <u>sternocleidomastoid muscle</u>.

* Ask the patient turn their head from side to side.

* <u>CN XI</u> palsy results in <u>weakness</u> in turning the head towards the <u>contralateral</u> side





> [!TIP]
> Muscular <u>atrophy</u> is a late sequelae of <u>CN XI</u> palsy. [[55]](/library/LJcwuW0)




#### Further evaluation




Consider further evaluation for underlying cause based on clinical findings. Studies may include:




* Imaging (i.e., <u>MRI</u> <u>orbit</u>, face, neck without and with IV contrast or CT neck with IV contrast): to evaluate for possible underlying compressive cause (e.g., <u>malignancy</u>) [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[18]](/library/UXbbxH)

* <u>Electromyography</u> (<u>EMG</u>): to assess severity of impairment





> [!TIP]
> <u>Accessory nerve palsy</u> should be part of the differential diagnosis of neck and shoulder <u>pain</u>. [[55]](/library/LJcwuW0)




### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and/or head and neck or plastic <u>surgery</u>.

* <u>Conservative measures</u> can be considered for patients with mild dysfunction and/or evidence of improvement on follow-up.  [[55]](/library/LJcwuW0)

* <u>Pain control</u> with <u>arm sling</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u> to strengthen <u>shoulder girdle</u> musculature

* Surgical measures (e.g., nerve grafting, neurolysis) [[55]](/library/LJcwuW0)[[56]](/library/aV1QGf0)

* May be preferred for acute traumatic causes with severe dysfunction

* Consider within 6 months of onset if there is poor response to <u>conservative management</u>

---

## Hypoglossal nerve palsy (XII)

### Etiology




* Tumors (e.g., <u>glomus jugulare</u>)

* Trauma

* <u>Occipital condyle fractures</u>, <u>skull base fractures</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> trauma (e.g., <u>neck dissection</u>, <u>endotracheal intubation</u>, <u>laryngeal mask airway</u>) [[57]](/library/XV19Gf0)

* Dissection of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>

* <u>Stroke</u>

* <u>Demyelination</u>





### Clinical features




* <u>Dysarthria</u>

* Difficulty <u>swallowing</u>

* <u>Atrophy</u> and <u>fasciculation</u> of the <u>tongue</u> on the side of the lesion





### Diagnostics [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)




#### <u>Cranial nerve examination</u>




Diagnosis is clinical, based on the <u>cranial nerve examination</u>. Ask the patient to:




* Press <u>tongue</u> against each cheek: Pressure to the cheek of the affected side might be increased.

* Stick out their <u>tongue</u>

* Deviation of the <u>tongue</u> to the <u>ipsilateral</u> side  when protruded due to <u>weakness</u> of the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>tongue</u> muscles.

* Signs of unilateral <u>lower motor neuron damage</u>: <u>tongue</u> <u>atrophy</u>, <u>fasciculations</u>, or asymmetry





![Hypoglossal nerve lesion](media/x7reojcs9zv7ck8g7v3nkaba.jpg)

Hypoglossal nerve lesion

![Innervation of the tongue](media/gcibn7youzj7ul56wsmy1yi1.jpg)

Innervation of the tongue




#### Further evaluation




Consider further evaluation to identify lesion location and underlying cause based on clinical findings. Studies may include:




* Imaging [[17]](/library/29cT5e0)[[18]](/library/UXbbxH)

* <u>MRI</u> head and neck (without and with IV contrast) : to locate nerve lesion and possible etiologies

* CT <u>skull base</u> and neck with IV contrast: may be performed in conjunction with <u>MRI</u> to evaluate the foramina and <u>skull base</u> (e.g., for <u>fractures</u>, <u>skull base</u> tumors)

* <u>Electromyography</u> (<u>EMG</u>): to assess severity of of nerve damage





### Treatment [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and speech language pathology.

* Consider early <u>surgery</u> in acute nerve injury. [[16]](/library/WV1Ptf0)

* Unilateral nerve injury

* May spontaneously resolve within 6 months.

* Advise patients to chew on the unaffected side.

* Bilateral nerve injury: Consider <u>enteral feeding</u> strategies for <u>swallowing</u> difficulty.

## Multiple cranial neuropathies

| <br>Overview of multiple <u>cranial</u> neuropathies [[58]](/library/xOaEuk)[[59]](/library/yOadEk)[[60]](/library/AOaREk)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | Affected <u>cranial nerve</u> | Cause | Clinical features |
| Chronic <u>meningitis</u> | <br>* Any<br><br> | <br><br>* Infection (<u>Lyme disease</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>cryptococcosis</u>)<br><br>* Inflammation (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>SLE</u>, <u>neoplasm</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Insidious or subacute <u>headache</u>, <u>fever</u>, and neck stiffness<br><br>* Additional symptoms depend on which CN is involved<br><br><br> |
| Jugular foramen syndrome | <br>* <u>CN IX</u>, <u>CN X</u>, and <u>CN XI</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Glomus tumor</u><br><br>* <u>Schwannoma</u><br><br>* <u>Meningioma</u><br><br>* <u>Metastatic</u> <u>tumor</u><br><br>* <u>Cholesteatoma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Loss of <u>taste</u> in the <u>posterior</u> third of the <u>tongue</u> (<u>CN IX</u>)<br><br>* Impaired speech and <u>swallowing</u>: <u>paralysis</u> of <u>vocal cords</u>, <u>palate</u>, and <u>pharyngeal muscles</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* Impaired head turning and shoulder elevation: <u>weakness</u> of the <u>trapezius</u> and <u>sternocleidomastoid muscles</u> (<u>CN XI</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Cavernous sinus syndrome</u> | <br>* <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, <u>CN V1</u>, <u>CN V2</u>, and <u>CN VI</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neoplasm</u> or inflammation (e.g., <u>Tolosa-Hunt</u> syndrome)<br><br>* Intracavernous <u>aneurysms</u><br><br>* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Impaired movement of the <u>eye</u>: <u>paralysis</u> of <u>extraocular muscles</u> (<u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, <u>CN VI</u>)<br><br>* <u>Horner syndrome</u><br><br>* Decreased sensation of the upper face (<u>CN V1</u>, <u>CN V2</u>)<br><br>* See “<u>Skull base syndromes</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Cerebellopontine angle syndrome</u> | <br>* <u>CN V</u>, <u>CN VI</u>, <u>CN VII</u>, <u>CN VIII</u>, <u>CN IX</u>, <u>CN X</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Neoplasms</u> of the <u>cerebellopontine angle</u><br><br>* <u>Vestibular schwannoma</u><br><br>* <u>Meningioma</u><br><br>* <u>Metastases</u><br><br>* <u>Cholesteatoma</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Impairment of facial sensation (<u>CN V</u>)<br><br>* <u>Tinnitus</u><br><br>* Progressive <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u><br><br>* <u>Gait disequilibrium</u><br><br>* <u>Vertigo</u> is uncommon.<br><br>* See “<u>Skull base syndromes</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u> | <br>* Any (most commonly <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN VII</u>, <u>CN IX</u>, <u>CN X</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Autoimmune inflammation of peripheral <u>cranial nerves</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Facial droop (<u>CN VII</u>)<br><br>* <u>Dysphonia</u>, <u>dysarthria</u>, and <u>dysphagia</u> (<u>CN IX</u> and <u>CN X</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ophthalmoplegia</u> and <u>diplopia</u> (<u>CN III</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Multiple sclerosis</u> | <br><br>* Any <u>cranial nerve</u> can be affected<br><br>* <u>CN II</u> impairment (<u>retrobulbar neuritis</u>) is a common feature<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Autoimmune inflammation of the <u>cranial nerves</u><br><br>* <u>Ischemic stroke</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vision loss</u> (<u>CN II</u>)<br><br>* <u>Internuclear ophthalmoplegia</u> (<u>INO</u>)<br><br><br> |
